content: Sciatica is a medical condition characterized by pain that radiates along the sciatic nerve, which extends from the lower back through the hips and down each leg. This pain often results from irritation or compression of the nerve roots forming the sciatic nerve, commonly due to herniated discs, spinal stenosis, or degenerative spine conditions. Symptoms typically include sharp, burning leg pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness, often affecting one side of the body. Understanding the underlying mechanisms highlights that sciatica is a form of radiculopathy caused by nerve root inflammation or mechanical pressure. Practical relevance includes its high prevalence as a cause of lower back and leg pain, impacting mobility and quality of life. Synonyms include lumbar radiculopathy and sciatic nerve pain, though 'sciatica' specifically refers to the symptom complex rather than a specific diagnosis. Limitations in diagnosis exist because similar symptoms may arise from peripheral neuropathies or vascular issues, so clinical evaluation is essential. Safety considerations emphasize that while sciatica often improves with conservative measures, severe cases with progressive weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction require immediate medical attention. This knowledge module provides comprehensive information on causes, symptoms, evaluation, management, lifestyle modifications, and safety, empowering informed decisions and communication with healthcare providers.

content: Sciatica refers to pain that originates from irritation or compression of the sciatic nerve or its roots in the lower spine. The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the human body, formed by nerve roots from L4, L5, S1, S2, and S3 spinal segments. Pain usually radiates from the lower back or buttock down the back of the thigh and leg to the foot. Sciatica is a symptom, not a diagnosis, often indicating underlying spine or nerve root problems such as herniated lumbar discs or spinal stenosis. Alternate terms include lumbar radiculopathy and sciatic nerve pain.

chunk_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Sciatic Nerve
content: The sciatic nerve is formed by the union of nerve roots emanating from the lower lumbar and sacral spine (L4-S3). It passes through the pelvis and travels down the posterior aspect of the thigh before branching into the tibial and common peroneal nerves near the knee. This nerve supplies motor and sensory fibers to most of the lower leg. Irritation or compression of its nerve roots leads to symptoms including pain, numbness, tingling (paresthesia), and muscle weakness in the regions served by the nerve.

content: Most cases of sciatica arise from mechanical compression or inflammation of lumbar or sacral nerve roots. Common causes include herniated or bulging intervertebral discs pressing on nerve roots, lumbar spinal stenosis (narrowing of spinal canal), spondylolisthesis (vertebra slipping forward), piriformis muscle syndrome (compression by pelvic muscle), or degenerative disc disease. Less common causes include tumors, infections, or trauma affecting the nerve.

content: Certain factors increase the likelihood of developing sciatica. These include advancing age (due to degenerative spinal changes), occupations involving heavy lifting or prolonged sitting, obesity (which increases mechanical stress on the spine), sedentary lifestyle, smoking (which impairs disc health), diabetes, and poor posture. Understanding risk factors helps guide prevention strategies.

content: Typical symptoms of sciatica include sharp, shooting, or burning pain radiating along the path of the sciatic nerve, usually in one leg. Patients often report numbness, tingling, or muscle weakness in the leg or foot. Symptoms can worsen with sitting, coughing, sneezing, or bending forward. Signs include positive straight leg raise test and decreased reflexes or strength in affected nerve root areas. Pain intensity and distribution can vary widely.

content: Diagnosis of sciatica relies primarily on clinical history and physical examination, focusing on neurological function and pain characteristics. Imaging studies like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) scans can identify herniated discs, spinal stenosis, or other anatomical causes. Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies may be used in complex cases to assess nerve function. It is important to rule out other causes such as vascular claudication or peripheral neuropathy.

content: Most sciatica cases improve with conservative treatment. This includes pain relief using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), physical therapy focusing on core strengthening and flexibility, activity modification, and sometimes short courses of oral corticosteroids. Heat or cold therapy and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) may provide symptom relief. Patient education on posture and ergonomics is essential. Evidence supports that many patients recover within weeks to months without surgery.

content: When conservative measures fail or symptoms worsen (e.g., progressive weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control), interventional approaches may be considered. These include epidural steroid injections to reduce nerve root inflammation or surgical options such as discectomy or laminectomy to relieve nerve compression. Surgery is typically reserved for severe or persistent symptoms and is generally effective in selected patients. Risks and benefits should be carefully discussed with healthcare providers.

content: Maintaining a healthy lifestyle helps manage and prevent sciatica recurrence. Regular low-impact exercise such as walking, swimming, or yoga improves spine flexibility and muscle strength. Avoiding prolonged sitting or heavy lifting, practicing good posture, and maintaining a healthy weight reduce strain on the lower back. Smoking cessation is recommended as it negatively affects spinal disc health. Educating patients about ergonomics at work and home is beneficial.

chunk_title: Safety Considerations and When to Seek Emergency Care
content: While sciatica is often benign, certain symptoms require urgent evaluation: sudden onset of severe weakness, numbness in the groin or genital area (saddle anesthesia), loss of bladder or bowel control, or worsening pain unrelieved by rest. These may indicate cauda equina syndrome, a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention to prevent permanent neurological damage. Patients should be aware of these red flags and seek prompt medical care if they arise.
